planting.note: Direct sow in fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing winter cold to naturally break seed dormancy for spring emergence; broadleaf milkweed forms a deep taproot and strongly resists transplanting once established.

directions: Broadleaf milkweed is a stout, upright native of shortgrass prairie and high desert grassland across the central and southwestern United States, from Nebraska and Kansas west to Utah and Nevada and south through Texas and Arizona into northern Mexico. Its broad, thick, wavy-margined gray-green leaves overlap so densely along the stem that the small, pale greenish-white flower clusters are almost hidden beneath the foliage — a distinctive silhouette unlike any other milkweed. It tolerates heat, drought, and alkaline or caliche soils that few other milkweed species can survive, making it a valuable monarch butterfly host plant for xeric gardens across the Great Plains and desert Southwest. Direct sow into permanent, well-drained locations in full sun; like most milkweeds, its deep taproot makes later transplanting very difficult.
sources: Xerces Society — Monarch Nectar Plant Guides

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing winter cold and moisture to naturally break seed dormancy; sand milkweed is adapted to shifting sandy soils and performs poorly in heavy clay or rich garden soil.

directions: Sand milkweed is an uncommon prairie native found in loose sand and sandy-loam soils from South Dakota and Wyoming south through Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, Colorado, New Mexico, and the Texas Panhandle. Densely woolly gray-green stems and broad, blunt-tipped leaves give the whole plant a soft, silvery texture, topped by rounded clusters of pale greenish-white flowers held in the leaf axils through summer. Like other milkweeds it serves as a larval host for monarch butterflies, and its tolerance of loose, infertile, wind-blown sand makes it a useful species for stabilizing sandy or dune-like garden sites where other milkweeds struggle. Choose a permanent, full-sun location with sharp drainage, since the deep taproot makes established plants nearly impossible to move.
sources: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service — Species Profile

subcategory: California native chaparral perennial pollinator wildflower

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in lean, fast-draining, rocky or gravelly soil in full sun to partial shade; heartleaf milkweed needs winter chilling and rainfall to break seed dormancy and goes summer-dormant after flowering in its native chaparral and foothill habitat.

directions: Heartleaf milkweed grows on dry, rocky slopes and open woodland edges of the Sierra Nevada foothills, southern Cascades, and Coast Ranges of California, Nevada, and Oregon, often emerging directly from crevices in decomposed granite or serpentine outcrops. Its blue-green, clasping, heart-shaped leaves and clusters of striking dark reddish-purple flowers distinguish it from other western milkweeds, and it tolerates more shade than most Asclepias species, growing naturally at the edge of oak woodland and chaparral. It is an important monarch butterfly host plant in the Sierra foothills, flowering from late spring into summer before going dormant with the onset of the dry California summer. Once established on a lean, well-drained site it is extremely drought tolerant and requires no supplemental summer water.
sources: Monarch Watch — Bring Back the Monarchs

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination, or cold-stratify seed indoors for 4 weeks before sowing; fan columbine is compact and clump-forming, well suited to rock gardens and border edges.

directions: Fan columbine is native to the mountain forests, cliffs, and open slopes of Japan, Korea, and far-eastern Siberia, where it grows at elevations up to 8,000 feet. It is among the most compact of all columbines, forming tidy clumps of thick, rounded, blue-green, fan-shaped leaflets topped by nodding, short-spurred flowers in violet-blue and creamy white — a shorter, sturdier growth habit than most North American species that makes it especially useful at the front of a shaded border or tucked into a rock garden. It thrives in cooler climates and appreciates afternoon shade and consistent moisture in warmer zones, going somewhat dormant if summer heat and drought are prolonged. Like other columbines it self-sows modestly and is a good early-season nectar source for bumblebees.

common_name: Nora Barlow Columbine (Double Pompom Heirloom Columbine)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination, or cold-stratify seed indoors for 3–4 weeks before a spring sowing, into humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade.

directions: Nora Barlow is a heritage double-flowered form of European columbine that has been grown in gardens for more than two centuries, named after Charles Darwin's granddaughter, who helped popularize it. Unlike the typical spurless, five-petaled columbine flower, its blooms are fully double — a dense pompom of narrow, quilled petals in shades of rose-pink and dusky red fading to green-tinged cream at the tips, with almost no visible spur. It comes substantially true from seed when grown in isolation from other columbines, though bees readily cross it with nearby Aquilegia, gradually producing intermediate, less-double offspring in a self-sown colony. Grow it as you would any European columbine, in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade, and allow some seed heads to mature each year to keep this old cottage-garden favorite going.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, gravelly soil in full sun to partial shade; scarlet larkspur needs the cool, moist winter and dry summer conditions of its native chaparral range to establish, going summer-dormant after flowering.

directions: Scarlet larkspur is native to coastal and inland chaparral slopes and canyon washes of southern California and northern Baja California, where its brilliant red, spurred flowers stand out sharply against the muted greens and grays of the surrounding scrub. Unlike the blues and purples typical of the genus, its vivid scarlet sepals and yellow-tipped petals are a striking adaptation for hummingbird pollination, and scarlet larkspur is one of the most reliably hummingbird-visited native wildflowers within its range. The deeply cut, fan-shaped basal leaves typically wither before the tall flowering stalk emerges in early summer; the plant then goes dormant through the dry chaparral summer, resprouting from a woody rootstock with fall rains. As with all delphiniums, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; seed requires an extended period of cold, moist stratification over winter to germinate the following spring, mimicking the natural Pacific Northwest prairie climate.

directions: Menzies' larkspur is a spring-blooming perennial of coastal bluffs, prairies, and oak woodland openings from British Columbia south through Washington and into northwestern Oregon, where it is a signature wildflower of the increasingly rare Pacific Northwest prairie ecosystem. Deeply cut, palmately lobed basal leaves give rise to loose spikes of rich violet-blue, spurred flowers in April and May, after which the plant goes dormant for the remainder of the year, disappearing entirely below ground through summer and winter. Because seed requires extended cold-moist stratification to break dormancy, direct sowing in fall is the most reliable propagation method, allowing natural winter chilling to trigger spring germination. Since Menzies' larkspur emerges and blooms so early and then vanishes completely, mark its location carefully to avoid disturbing the dormant rootstock during the rest of the year.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in mild-winter climates or early spring where winters are severe, into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; scarify or soak seed overnight in warm water to improve germination of this small-seeded annual lupine.

directions: Miniature lupine is one of the smallest and most widespread native lupines of western North America, found from British Columbia to Baja California across grasslands, coastal bluffs, and open woodlands, often carpeting entire hillsides in dense, low drifts each spring. Its diminutive size — often just a few inches tall — belies its outsized impact in a wildflower planting, where masses of tiny, bicolor blue-and-white pea flowers combine beautifully with California poppy and other classic California native annual companions. As a nitrogen-fixing legume it improves the soil it grows in, and it completes its entire life cycle in a single cool season, self-sowing reliably where conditions suit it. It requires no supplemental water or fertilizer once seedlings are established, making it an easy, low-maintenance choice for meadow and slope wildflower mixes.

planting.note: Scarify seed by nicking the seed coat, then direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination, into lean, well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; silvery lupine develops a deep taproot and strongly resists transplanting once established.

directions: Silvery lupine is a widespread perennial of sagebrush steppe, montane meadows, and open forests across the intermountain West, ranging from the southern Canadian Rockies south through Colorado, Utah, and Arizona at elevations up to 10,000 feet. Its common name comes from the fine, silvery hairs that cover the palmately compound leaves and stems, giving the whole plant a soft, silver-gray cast that contrasts nicely with its spikes of blue-violet, pea-shaped flowers through summer. As a nitrogen-fixing legume adapted to lean, dry mountain soils, it is an important component of high-elevation rangeland restoration and pollinator seed mixes, providing forage for native bees and serving as a larval host for several regional blue butterflies. Once established from a deep taproot it is extremely drought tolerant and long-lived, requiring no supplemental water or fertility in appropriate dry, well-drained sites.
sources: US Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)
